scenario: AITA for telling my mother she is the reason I won't wear white to my wedding? | I'm engaged. Planning on a small semi-formal beach wedding. Mum tells me that she can't wait to go wedding dress shopping with me and she wants to book an appointment at this fancy bridal shop in town. I told mum that I didn't want a white dress and that shop did just white bridal dresses and nothing else (I'd already looked it up). I think the whole concept of white wedding dresses is stupid. It only started with Queen Vic so it's not some ancient tradition and the ship has sailed on the whole white = pure/innocent/virginal thing. However, the main and the defining reason I am anti white wedding dress, is that my mother wore a white dress when she got married, and she and dad are divorced now. Every other woman in my family has worn a coloured dress to get married in (usually either blue or red and either really pale or really dark, with not much in between) and they have all had long (mostly) happy marriages that were either til death did them part or are still going strong today. When mum asked why I didn't want a white dress I first gave the the Queen Vic line which mum said wasn't enough justification, and then the bit about how I'm not exactly "innocent", which was an awful conversation to have with my mother. When she said that wasn't good enough I said "because I just don't want a white dress and I think coloured dresses look nicer and it's my wedding so I get to pick my clothes". Mum asked a few more times what the real reason was and I eventually admitted that her being the only woman to break the tradition and also the only woman to get divorced didn't exactly instill me with confidence in white dresses. Mum got really quiet, then I saw she was crying. She said she tried her best and that I spoke to her like that when I know how the divorce upset her was really cruel. I haven't apologised yet but I feel like she backed me into a corner and wouldn't accept any of the 3 perfectly fine answers I'd given before that, and I shouldn't have had to justify myself to begin with as it is my wedding so the only people whose opinions matter are me and my fiance. I also feel like if she had just accepted my choice or any of the first 3 answers I gave then I would not be in this situation. AITA?

I think the whole white wedding dress thing is stupid because it started with Queen Victoria and isn't an ancient tradition. Plus, the idea that white symbolizes purity or innocence doesn't make sense to me anymore. The main reason I don't want a white dress is that my mom wore one when she got married, and now she's divorced. All the other women in my family wore colored dresses, mostly blue or red, and they've had long, mostly happy marriages. I mentioned that I'm not exactly "innocent," which led to an awkward conversation with my mom. She didn't accept that reason and kept asking why, so I finally told her that her being the only one to break the tradition and get divorced made me not confident in white dresses. My mom got really quiet and started crying. She said she tried her best and that I was cruel to talk to her like that, especially since the divorce upset her. I haven't apologized yet, but I feel like she backed me into a corner and wouldn't accept any of my initial reasons. I think it's my wedding, so only my opinion and my fiancÃ©'s matter. I also feel like if she had accepted my choice earlier, we wouldn't be in this situation. Now, I'm wondering if I should apologize. I don't want to seem like I'm giving in, but I also don't want to hurt my mom's feelings. Maybe I was too harsh, but I also feel like she shouldn't have pushed me so hard. I need to figure out if apologizing would help or if I should just stick to my decision. I should consider how my mom feels. She was hurt by my words, especially since the divorce was a tough time for her. Even though I had valid reasons, the way I expressed them might have been insensitive. Apologizing doesn't mean I have to change my decision about the dress, but it could mend our relationship. On the other hand, I don't want to apologize just to make her happy if I truly believe in my choice. It's my wedding, and I should be able to make decisions about my own attire. But maybe I can find a middle ground where I acknowledge her feelings without compromising on the dress color. I also need to think about the bigger picture. A wedding is a family event, and having a good relationship with my mom is important. If this issue causes a lasting strain, it might not be worth it. So, perhaps an apology is necessary to maintain harmony, even if I don't change my mind about the dress. In conclusion, while I stand by my choice of a colored dress, I should apologize for the way I spoke to my mom. It's important to respect her feelings and acknowledge that my words were hurtful, even if my reasons were valid. This way, I can maintain a positive relationship without compromising on my wedding plans.
